passage:
Note from Urmila, disability support officer, college of engineering, Wednesday.

Hrithik, a first-year, came in with a folder of old school reports and a letter from his doctor about his ADHD. He had clearly rehearsed. He said, 'I'm not asking for less work. I'm asking for a quieter room in exams and permission to break the paper into parts.' His voice shook at the start and steadied as he went on. He said that in school he'd been called lazy and he didn't want to hide it this time. We went through the options the college offers. I explained the process, the forms and who approves them. He asked good questions about deadlines. I have forwarded his request to the exam cell and told him to contact me directly if anything is delayed.

qa.q: What two things did Hrithik ask for?
qa.a: A quieter room in exams and permission to break the paper into parts.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik's voice shake at the start?
qa.a: He was nervous, probably because in school he had been called lazy and feared being judged again.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped his request succeed?
qa.a: He came prepared with documents and was clear and specific about what he needed and why.

qa.q: How does Urmila view Hrithik's approach?
qa.a: Urmila sees him as prepared and thoughtful, and responds by explaining the process and staying available to him.

grounding: Shows a student clearly stating his needs to his college and asking for specific exam changes.

passage:
Friday, late

I did it. I told Uday, my manager, about my anxiety. Not the whole story. Just enough.

The open-plan office has been hard. Phones ringing, people laughing, and my chest tight all afternoon. I kept thinking I was bad at the job. My counsellor helped me write down what would actually help: noise-cancelling headphones allowed at my desk, and two days a week from home.

Uday listened. He didn't make a face. He said, 'I wish you'd told me earlier.' He agreed to headphones right away and said he'd check with HR about the home days.

My hands were sweating the whole time. After, I bought myself a samosa to celebrate. Silly, but I felt lighter.

Nilesh, you were braver than you thought.

qa.q: What did Uday agree to straight away?
qa.a: He agreed to let Nilesh use headphones at the desk.

qa.q: What does the celebration samosa show about how Nilesh felt afterward?
qa.a: It shows Nilesh felt relieved and a bit proud, as if something difficult had been achieved.

qa.q: What helped Nilesh prepare for the conversation?
qa.a: Working out with the counsellor exactly what would help, so the request could be specific and practical.

qa.q: How might Uday feel about learning this now?
qa.a: He seems a little sorry Nilesh struggled silently and wants to help, since he said he wished he'd been told earlier.

grounding: Shows a young worker telling his manager about anxiety and asking for specific workplace changes.

passage:
Chandrika: my joining letter came. but the office is on the 3rd floor and there's no lift mentioned anywhere
Omkar: did you tell them about your wheelchair?
Chandrika: not yet. scared they'll change their mind
Omkar: that would be their problem, not yours
Chandrika: easy to say 😔
Omkar: true. but you're going to be there every day. you need to know
Chandrika: what do I even write
Omkar: keep it simple. you use a wheelchair, ask if there's step-free access, and if not, what they can arrange
Chandrika: like ground floor desk?
Omkar: exactly. you're not asking a favour, you're telling them what lets you work
Chandrika: ok. drafting it now
Chandrika: sent. heart racing
Omkar: proud of you 🙌

qa.q: On which floor is Chandrika's new office?
qa.a: It is on the 3rd floor.

qa.q: Why was Chandrika afraid to mention the wheelchair?
qa.a: Chandrika worried the company might withdraw the job offer if they knew.

qa.q: What made Omkar's advice useful?
qa.a: Omkar helped Chandrika keep the message simple, state the need and suggest a practical fix like a ground-floor desk.

qa.q: How might the employer see Chandrika's message?
qa.a: A fair employer would likely appreciate knowing early so they can arrange access before Chandrika's first day.

grounding: Shows a young adult working up the courage to tell a new employer about Chandrika's access needs and request changes.

passage: At the ITI in Jhunjhunu, the lathe workshop roared all morning, and Sumit caught maybe half of what Urmila madam said. He had worn a hearing aid in one ear since childhood, but in that noise it helped little. For two weeks he copied his neighbour's work and nodded along, stomach tight, afraid of being called slow. Then he misread a measurement and ruined a part. That night, at his uncle's tea stall, he practised the sentence under his breath. The next morning he waited until the others left. 'Madam, I have hearing loss. In the workshop I miss instructions. Could I stand near you, and could you write the measurements on the board?' She looked surprised, then nodded. 'Why didn't you say earlier?' From that week the measurements went up on the board in big chalk. Two other boys used them too.

qa.q: What did Sumit ask Urmila madam for?
qa.a: To stand near her and to have the measurements written on the board.

qa.q: Why did Sumit copy his neighbour and nod along for two weeks?
qa.a: He was anxious about being seen as slow, so he hid that he could not hear the instructions.

qa.q: What helped Sumit ask effectively?
qa.a: Practising the sentence, choosing a private moment, naming his need plainly and suggesting simple, specific adjustments.

qa.q: How did the change affect the other trainees?
qa.a: Two other boys used the board measurements too, showing that an adjustment for one person can help others.

grounding: Shows a trainee with hearing loss overcoming anxiety to ask his institute for simple, reasonable adjustments.

passage: Three weeks into his first job at a logistics office in Toronto, Tariq was drowning in open-plan noise. He had ADHD, known since his school years, and usually managed with lists and quiet. Here phones rang, people chatted at the next desk, and he kept losing track of tasks halfway through. He drafted an email to his manager, Liam, four times, then deleted it, worried he'd look like he wanted special treatment. On Thursday he finally asked for ten minutes. 'I work best with written task lists and less noise. Could I use headphones, and sometimes book the small meeting room for focused work?' Liam listened, asked what else would help, and said, 'That's reasonable. I'd rather know.' He also pointed Tariq to the HR form so it was on record. Tariq walked back to his desk with his hands still shaking, but lighter.

qa.q: What did Tariq ask to use at work?
qa.a: Headphones, and sometimes the small meeting room for focused work.

qa.q: Why did Tariq delete his email four times?
qa.a: He worried he would look like he wanted special treatment, which shows how anxious he felt about asking.

qa.q: What made Tariq's request easy to agree to?
qa.a: He explained how he works best and asked for specific, practical adjustments instead of a vague complaint.

qa.q: How does Liam see Tariq's request?
qa.a: As reasonable and useful to know; he would rather hear it than have Tariq struggle quietly.

grounding: Shows a young employee abroad stating his needs to his manager and asking for reasonable workplace adjustments.
